extracted.intended_audience: newspaper reporters and journalism students (cub reporters)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidelines and standards for composing newspaper news stories, covering leads, the body, legal cautions, style (clarity, tone, sentence length), and handling editorial policies. Aimed at teaching reporters how to produce accurate, interesting copy for daily papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Boxed summaries at story start
rubrics_metrics.description: When a story is complicated and the number of details numerous, or when important points or facts need particular emphasis, it is customary to make a digest of the principal items and box them in display type before the regular lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determined by city editor and copy readers but reporters may suggest them; common for accidents (lists of dead/injured in bold), important athletic events (records, attendance, gate receipts), speeches, trials, executions (epigrams, important utterances), international diplomatic letters (main points), lengthy governmental reports. If in doubt, prepare a separate boxed summary and leave it for the city editor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summarizing lead (summary lead)
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead that summarizes the essential facts of the story — definite, answers who, what, when, where, why, and how.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommended for beginners because it is definite and easier to judge whether it succeeds; rely on the excellence of the news to carry the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal (suspense/human-interest) lead
rubrics_metrics.description: Begins with a question, bit of verse, startling quotation, or one or two manifestly unimportant details that tell little yet whet the reader's appetite, leading to the main point later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More difficult than summarizing leads; used to make attractive news that lacks inherent interest (old, commonplace, or distant news). Requires originality of approach and statement; must compensate for poverty of news by being more attractive, striking, or piquant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question lead
rubrics_metrics.description: An informal lead that opens with a question to entice the reader into the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to provoke curiosity; examples illustrate method of enticing reader and then supplying context or precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse lead
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead beginning with a bit of verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: More difficult because most writers are uncertain writing metrical lines; can work but requires skill; example given with sailors' plea for mail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary-statement lead
rubrics_metrics.description: An informal lead beginning with an extraordinary statement made by a person in a speech, interview, or trial scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective when the quotation is striking; if the quoted statement is so long or summarizes the whole story, it becomes a summarizing lead instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspense lead
rubrics_metrics.description: A lead that purposely begins with unimportant but enticing details and lures the reader onward, holding out a half-promise of something worthwhile later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most difficult informal lead type; powerful when well handled; used to tempt readers to the middle or end before revealing the main point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead should suggest tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a lead that will suggest the tone of the story (pathetic, tragic, humorous, mildly satirical, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads that match the intended tone increase story success; examples contrast pathetic/tragic vs half-serious humor. Tone is discussed further in subsequent chapters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beginner's advice on leads
rubrics_metrics.description: Beginners are advised initially to attempt only the summarizing lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarizing leads are definite and measurable; informal leads involve effects (climax, suspense) that novices are unlikely to achieve consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary goals for the body: accuracy and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reporter has written a strong lead, the body should be a simple narration of events in chronological order with explanation or description, maintaining interest and accuracy. The two 'crimes' are inaccuracy and dullness, with inaccuracy the greater.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and arrange details wisely; organization makes follow-through easier. Final test of a story is its effect upon the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid inventing or premature conclusions (accuracy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not draw on imagination or jump too readily to conclusions to make a story better; presenting unverified statements as facts harms the paper and innocent people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences include humiliation when corrected, loss of public confidence, and legal injury to individuals. Examples: wildly incorrect casualty lists after disasters; staff dismissals and libel judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the law of libel
rubrics_metrics.description: Every newspaper person should know the law of libel: who may be held responsible and what constitutes libel (published matter that tends to disgrace, degrade, or subject a person to public distrust, ridicule, or contempt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners, publisher, editor, writer, and even sellers can be liable if awareness is proved. Sarcasm or irony implying reproach can be libelous. Intent is not a defense; proven injury results in damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of libel (attribution and qualifying phrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: When making potentially unpleasing statements about a person, give the name of the source making the charge or avoid specific charges by inserting qualifying phrases such as 'it is alleged', 'it is rumored', 'it is charged'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A story reads more convincingly when the reporter's authority is given; the example demonstrates skilful avoidance of outright accusation in a shoplifting arrest story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration; favor understatement
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggerated statements defeat their end; understatement is preferred because it preserves reader confidence for when large figures/facts must be asserted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consistent understatement builds credibility; leading papers avoid unverified or exaggerated statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid editorializing in news copy
rubrics_metrics.description: Present news from as unbiased a standpoint as possible; avoid letting personal views color news articles — editorial columns are for opinion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: News columns should be 'colorless' presentation of facts. Example of a politically charged, biased story that was not printed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe newspaper editorial policies and expected bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters must learn and observe their paper's editorial policies, since modern newspapers are businesses with policies set by owners that may include crusades or preferred angles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers may slant coverage in line with campaigns (e.g., against pawnshops); reporters should feature what editors request. This may require sympathetic or severe emphasis as directed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow editors' commands precisely
rubrics_metrics.description: When the managing or city editor directs how to treat a story (especially political/civic measures), the reporter must see and write as requested or seek another position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Occasional forced departures from personal conviction occur; obeying commands is necessary for success on the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness in the body
rubrics_metrics.description: Every paragraph must be clear; its relation to other paragraphs evident; the story as a whole should be understandable with minimal mental effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep connected ideas together; separate incidents separated in time; maintain consistent verb tenses; include sufficient summary of preceding events when writing follow-ups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Four ways to obtain coherence within a story: (1) arrangement of facts in natural sequence; (2) use of pronouns; (3) repetition; (4) relation words/phrases/clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proper grouping and logical arrangement are primary; pronouns and skillful repetition are especially effective. Example fire story shows repetition to hold ideas in sequence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use relation words sparingly in news writing
rubrics_metrics.description: News prose tends to use few connectives (moreover, finally, on the other hand) because editors and readers demand ideas that follow closely and compressed thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This contributes to the 'bing-bing-bing' rapid narrative style valued for emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware overuse of 'bing-bing-bing' short-sentence style
rubrics_metrics.description: The short, punchy, connective-poor style helps rapid narrative and emotional excitement but, indulged too freely, produces a fitful, choppy effect that is not good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sentences should be longer and more varied in construction than constant short sentences; use the style selectively for effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis through precise language and tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis is achieved by avoidance of vague literary phrasing, by due regard for tone, and by condensation of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid grandiloquent, sonorous phrases that mean little; such vagueness destroys tone. Tone and precision overlap; both are needed for forceful presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague literary phrasing and affected diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not adopt worn-out or expansive literary expressions to appear literary; they are often vague and hazily expressive when transplanted into news copy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show bloated, clichéd endings or overwrought scenic description that repel rather than engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Watch for unintended humorous or absurd juxtapositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Careless proximity of unrelated ideas or awkward phrasing can create unintended humor or absurdity that destroys intended tone (e.g., indignified or unintended double meanings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proofread for unfortunate closeness of unrelated ideas; ensure wording doesn't create unintended implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varied sentence length; aim for medium length
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for a happy medium in sentence length with a tendency toward shorter sentences than in other kinds of writing; about twenty words is a good average.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid markedly short (monotonous, choppy) or unnecessarily long (heavy, tiresome) sentences. Remember broad readership including less-educated readers; make prose fluent and easy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Condense ideas into the smallest space possible; diffuse style is never forceful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the space allotted by the city editor precisely; if allotted more space than needed, add meaningful additional details rather than padding with words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final test: effect upon the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: The final test of the goodness of a story is its effect upon the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the story attains the desired result (accuracy and interest) without conforming to standard patterns, it still may establish a new successful pattern. Get accuracy and interest by whatever method works.
